reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: The most common porphyria of childhood, arising from deficient ferrochelatase, the final enzyme of haem biosynthesis, causing protoporphyrin accumulation
Hallmark is acute, painful, non-blistering photosensitivity beginning within minutes of sun exposure, with burning, stinging, redness and swelling rather than vesicles
Because symptoms are pain and swelling rather than obvious rash, diagnosis is often delayed for years and children may be labelled as behavioural sun-avoiders
Chronic changes include waxy skin thickening and shallow scarring over exposed areas, notably the knuckles and nose
A subset develop protoporphyrin-related cholestatic liver disease, which can progress to acute, potentially fatal hepatic failure
Diagnosis is made by markedly raised free erythrocyte (and plasma) protoporphyrin; urinary porphyrins are typically normal because protoporphyrin is not water soluble
Most cases are due to biallelic loss-of-function or a hypomorphic ferrochelatase allele; an X-linked variant results from gain-of-function ALAS2 mutations

Management principles centre on strict sunlight avoidance and photoprotection, correction of any iron deficiency, and monitoring for hepatobiliary complications; specific therapies aiming to increase sun tolerance are available
Mild microcytic anaemia and gallstones (protoporphyrin-rich) are recognised associations
reference.pathophysiology: Erythropoietic protoporphyria is caused by reduced activity of ferrochelatase, which inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX to form haem. Deficient enzyme activity, usually from a loss-of-function mutation combined with a common low-expression allele, leads to accumulation of metal-free protoporphyrin, predominantly in developing erythroid cells. Circulating protoporphyrin absorbs visible light (around 400 nm), generating reactive oxygen species in the dermal microvasculature and producing the immediate, painful phototoxic reaction. Because protoporphyrin is lipophilic it is excreted in bile rather than urine, and excess biliary protoporphyrin can precipitate, forming gallstones and, in some patients, causing progressive cholestatic liver injury. The X-linked form is caused by gain-of-function ALAS2 mutations that overproduce the precursor pool.
additionalDifferentials: Solar urticaria and polymorphic light eruption
Other cutaneous porphyrias (porphyria cutanea tarda, variegate porphyria)
additionalInvestigations: Free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (markedly elevated) with fractionation to confirm metal-free protoporphyrin
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging to detect protoporphyric liver disease
Iron studies, as iron deficiency can worsen the disorder
Molecular genetic testing of the ferrochelatase gene and, in the X-linked variant, ALAS2
redFlags: Rising liver enzymes or jaundice heralding protoporphyric hepatopathy or acute liver failure
Severe photosensitivity reactions with marked pain and swelling after minimal exposure
Signs of decompensated cholestatic liver disease requiring transplant evaluation
reference.prognosis: Photosensitivity is lifelong but manageable with rigorous sun avoidance, and most patients maintain a good quality of life with photoprotection. The major threat to prognosis is protoporphyric liver disease, which affects a minority but can progress rapidly to hepatic failure requiring transplantation; bone marrow transplantation may be needed to correct the underlying overproduction.
pitfalls: Ordering only urinary porphyrins, which are normal, and wrongly excluding porphyria
Dismissing painful photosensitivity without a rash as functional or behavioural
Failing to monitor liver function over time
Overlooking iron deficiency, which can aggravate the condition
Assuming standard sunscreens give adequate protection against visible light
